title: Cache key entropy & hash partitioning design review — Cascade Systems
summary: Deep technical review of prefix/prompt cache key design, hash partitioning for multi-tenant safety, hit rate expectations, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed on tenant-prefixed namespaces + salted hashing, conservative TTLs, and follow-up benchmarks to validate hit-rate/latency tradeoffs. Action items: run bench, share config snippet, and propose eviction/fairness policy.
action_items: Maya Singh — run KV cache benchmark at 5k QPS with 16-token avg prompts and 30% repeated prefixes — due 2025-09-05
Jordan Lee (Cascade) — provide representative prefix distribution CSV (top 10k prefixes with frequency) — due 2025-08-29
Alex Monroe — share Redwood config snippet for per-tenant namespace + salted key examples + suggested eviction policy — due 2025-08-25
next_steps: Cascade shares prefix distribution and PII gating requirements
Follow-up 30-min sync to review bench results and recommend shard counts (scheduled tentatively week of 2025-09-08)
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-08-22 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 1h08m
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood SE), Jordan (Cascade Infra), Priya (Cascade Platform), Samir (Cascade SRE), Elena (Cascade Product)

Auto-generated sections: Summary: (see metadata)

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll get started. um the goal today is to walk through how Cascade is thinking about prefix caching and where Redwood's KV/prefix strategies map on to your constraints.
[00:18] Jordan: yep thanks. to set context, our main workload is real-time policy generation for config flows, average prompt length ~14 tokens after tokenizer, high QPS spikes up to 7k, multi-tenant (hundreds of tenants) with a hot tail of a few customers.
[00:35] Maya: got it. curious first — what hit rates are you seeing today with your prototype?
[00:41] Samir: right now it's, uh, naive: we normalize by trimming whitespace and lowercasing only, we see about 8–12% hit rate on hashes, but a lot of that is collisions and accidental key leakage across tenants because we didn't namespace properly.
[00:59] Diego: note — some transcriber may show K-V as K V, sorry for the noise.
[01:05] Alex: yeah and that matters. for multi-tenant safety our recommended starting point is per-tenant namespaces plus a salted hash so keys are not guessable. that prevents cross-tenant accidental visibility and gives you the option to shard by tenant id.
[01:25] Priya: when you say salted hash, do you mean a global salt inside Redwood Dedicate — sorry Dedicated — or per-tenant salt? we have a compliance requirement that tenant data must be cryptographically separated.
[01:38] Maya: good question. there are tradeoffs: per-tenant salt is safest but increases metadata slightly; global salt plus strict namespace prefix still keeps keys segregated, but if someone gains access to the salt it erodes separation. typical enterprise approach we see is per-tenant salt stored in KMS, rotated quarterly.
[01:57] Jordan: ok we have HSM-backed KMS in our VPC, so per-tenant keying is doable.
[02:05] Alex: excellent. on the key format itself we suggest normalized-prompt -> canonicalization -> truncated fingerprint. canonicalization includes removing ephemeral timestamps, standardizing numbers, and optionally removing non-deterministic tokens (e.g., request ids). truncation to 128-bit fingerprint for storage efficiency.
[02:27] Samir: truncation worries me — collisions at 128-bit are astronomically low, but our dataset is big across tenants, should we use 256?
[02:36] Maya: 128 is usually fine for practical TTL sizes and cache sizes we see, but if you prefer a larger digest we can switch to 256 at the cost of memory overhead. we also recommend including tenant_id in the preimage to avoid cross-tenant collisions entirely.
[02:55] Elena: what about prefix variants — e.g., small templated changes cause misses. do you recommend aggressive normalization or conservative?
[03:03] Diego: that's a workload question. if you normalize too aggressively you risk merging semantically different prompts; if too conservative hit-rates suffer. common pattern: apply a lightweight normalizer (lowercase, normalize whitespace, strip repeated punctuation) and optionally a semantic hashing layer for pre-known templates (embedding clustering).
[03:24] Jordan: we do have a set of ~120 templates used by 70% of traffic. maybe template-aware keys would help.
[03:31] Maya: absolutely. you can detect template matches at the router and synthesize a template-id + slot-hash key which massively increases hit rate for template-driven flows.
[03:39] [03:40] Alex: moving to partitioning — consistent hashing across shards so that a tenant's keys map to stable shards reduces cache churn during scaling events. two main options: tenant-affinity sharding (dedicated shard per heavyweight tenant) or pooled shards with consistent hash ring.
[03:54] Priya: we want fairness and no noisy-neighbor. heavy tenants have caused thrashing in our other caches.
[04:01] Maya: sounds like a hybrid approach fits: give heavy tenants dedicated shard ranges and pool the rest. Redwood's runtime supports tenant pinning policy and automatic fallback if dedicated shards are full.
[04:14] Samir: what's the overhead for maintaining the hash ring?
[04:18] Diego: negligible at runtime with a top-level router library. the complexity comes in rebalancing during rolling upgrades — that's why we recommend consistent hashing with virtual nodes to reduce movement.
[04:29] Alex: important metric discipline: measure key cardinality per tenant, 95th percentile key lookup latency, miss amplification (how many redundant sub-requests on miss), and per-tenant memory occupancy. those inform shard sizing.
[04:46] Jordan: can you explain miss amplification?
[04:48] Maya: sure. miss amplification is when one logical miss triggers multiple work items (e.g., recomputing embeddings, model queries, and caching them) — it increases downstream load. so on misses we prioritize fast fallback to a cheaper model variant rather than re-compute heavy work synchronously.
[05:05] Priya: okay. eviction policy — do you recommend LRU or segmented LRU?
[05:10] Alex: for multi-tenant fairness segmented LRU or clock with tenant quotas works better. you can combine a global LRU with per-tenant soft quotas to avoid a single tenant evicting everything.
[05:21] Elena: how do we detect hot keys and protect them?
[05:23] Maya: hot key protection usually uses write-through registries or frequency counters (TinyLFU) and optionally pinning keys. for prefix caches pinning model responses for top-N prefixes increases hit rate predictability.
[05:36] [05:38] Samir: we noticed in our prototype bloom filters gave false positives and weird behavior when we rotated shards. any guidance?
[05:44] Diego: Bloom filters are useful to filter cold misses but with partitioned stores you need per-shard filters and careful reset semantics during rehashing. counting bloom filters help with deletes but add space. we typically avoid bloom filters for mutable caches used in production unless necessary.
[06:01] Jordan: regarding metrics, what's an achievable hit rate for template-heavy workloads?
[06:06] Maya: with template-aware keys + salted per-tenant namespace + small TTLs (5–15m) we've seen 40–60% effective hit rates on the hot path in similar customers. naive normalization only is usually sub-15%.
[06:21] Priya: latency improvements — are we talking 10ms or 100ms?
[06:25] Alex: depends on where cache is located. an in-process or host-local cache (local SSD or RAM) can yield single-digit ms p50 improvements; networked cache (shared across GPUs) yields ~20–40ms p50 but much higher throughput. for your latency SLO of 100ms p95, networked cache with TTL tuning is acceptable.
[06:44] Samir: on-prem constraint — we have limited RAM per host and we prefer host-local caching. how do you handle KV replication for availability?
[06:53] Diego: for on-prem we recommend a two-tier cache: small host-local LRU for p50 fast hits + regional shared cache for larger capacity and cross-host hits. replication can be async with write-back to shared store; it's a tradeoff between consistency and latency.
[07:12] [07:15] Jordan: that adds complexity for eviction coordination.
[07:18] Maya: yes, but instrumentation helps. Redwood's console exposes per-host hit rates, cross-host miss rates, and tail latency to tune the balance.
[07:28] Elena: what about quantization effects on cache keys? any surprises?
[07:33] Alex: quantization mainly affects model outputs, not keys. but if you use model-derived embeddings for semantic hashing the embedding instability across quantization levels can reduce hit rates. solution: compute embedding keys using a stable quantized-aware encoder or keep embedding computation on a single higher-precision host and reuse those keys.
[07:52] Priya: interesting. we also want to understand cache warm strategies for blue-green deploys.
[07:57] Maya: warm by replaying recent hot prefixes during deploy, or proactive prefetch based on traffic windows. Redwood supports warmup hooks in the control plane so you can push top-N prefixes into new shards before cutover.
[08:12] Samir: do you have recommendations for TTL?
[08:15] Diego: start conservative: 5–15 minutes for dynamic prompts, 1–6 hours for templated content. monitor accuracy drift; TTLs tie directly to freshness requirements.
[08:27] Jordan: on multi-tenant safety: suppose a noisy tenant starts hammering the cache with slightly varied prefixes to fill the store — how do we protect?
[08:36] Maya: enforce per-tenant insertion rate limits, shard pinning for heavy tenants, and background eviction that favors frequently accessed keys across tenants. also, maintain admission control: probabilistic admission (TinyLFU-like) avoids beginners from flooding cache with one-offs.
[08:53] Alex: add to that: audit logs. you need to correlate insert patterns with tenant ids and potentially throttle at the router. all of that must appear in your SRE dashboards.
[09:04] Elena: audit logs — we need to surface who evicted what for compliance. feasible?
[09:09] Diego: yes but at scale you sample. full eviction logs are expensive; instead store aggregated eviction stats per tenant and sample the evictions that triggered alerts.
[09:21] [09:22] Priya: on privacy: does Redwood ever store prompt text in long-lived caches?
[09:27] Alex: we recommend storing fingerprints only for long-term caches. raw prompts can be in ephemeral caches (in-memory) and not persisted. for regulated customers we can operate in a zero-text retention mode by default.
[09:41] Jordan: good. for our on-prem deployment we want zero retained prompt text outside of the customer's VPC. is that supported?
[09:48] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports that — your cache lives in your VPC or on-prem, and we can provide options to never log raw prompts and to keep only hashed keys.
[09:58] Alex: quick note on monitoring and benching — measure requests per second, unique keys per minute, hit/miss ratio, time wasted on recompute, and p95 end-to-end latency. those will drive shard sizing and eviction policy.
[10:12] Samir: what about memory accounting per key? do we store response and metadata separately?
[10:17] Diego: typically stored as value blob + metadata (tenant id, ttl, last accessed). value size varies, often you compress model outputs (snappy) and store compressed blobs; that helps with memory pressure.
[10:29] Priya: any gotchas with cross-region caches?
[10:33] Maya: cross-region replication introduces checksum drift and replication lag. use region-local caches for latency critical paths and async replication for analytics and longer TTLs.
[10:45] [10:46] Jordan: can you summarize recommended immediate config for our pilot?
[10:49] Alex: yes: 1) per-tenant namespace + per-tenant salt via your KMS, 2) canonicalizer that strips timestamps and normalizes whitespace, 3) template-id path for top templates, 4) hybrid shard strategy: dedicate shards to top 5 heavy tenants, pool the rest on consistent hash ring, 5) segmented LRU with per-tenant soft quotas, 6) TTLs: 5–15m dynamic, 1–6h templated, 7) host-local + shared regional cache two-tier setup for on-prem.
[11:20] Elena: sounds good.
[11:22] Maya: we'll run the bench and produce a hit-rate projection with p50/p95 latency implications.
[11:28] Samir: and we'll provide the prefix distribution file.
[11:31] Alex: cool — any other questions?
[11:33] Priya: one more: can you share a sample key schema and router config?
[11:37] Alex: yes I'll share a snippet after the call.
[11:41] Diego: one operational caveat — when rehashing shards, plan maintenance windows, and use virtual nodes to minimize movement.
[11:48] Jordan: noted.
[11:50] Alex: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the config, bench results, and a proposed pilot timeline.
[11:58] End of transcript (truncating for brevity).
